card.name: Mussoll
card.tagline: A rhythmic pestle-dance of victory and dynastic memory in the village of Chandor.
card.profile: Mussoll, also known as Mussllam khell, is a historic folk dance performed by the Christian Kshatriya community in Chandor, Goa. The dance utilizes heavy wooden pestles as both props and rhythmic instruments to commemorate historical military victories and dynastic shifts. It follows a ritualized path from the village church—built on the site of an ancient Shiva temple—to the yards of local residences. Accompanied by the ghumot drum and a participant dressed as a bear, the dancers execute a synchronized pounding motion that simulates the processing of grain while singing oral histories.
card.insight: Dancers in Chandor carry heavy wooden pestles fitted with internal metal blades that jingle as they strike the ground, a sound that has echoed through the village since the 14th-century Kadamba era.
card.profile_long:
The village of Chandor, once the capital of the Kadamba dynasty known as Chandrapur, serves as the exclusive site for the preservation of Mussoll. This dance is a complex layer of Goan history, blending memories of the Satavahana, Kadamba, and Vijayanagara periods. One historical account attributes the dance's inception to King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire, who is said to have performed it in 1390 to celebrate the conquest of the Chandrapur fort from a Chola ruler. Other traditions suggest the songs are even older, dating back to the Satavahana era, with later rulers adding hymns of praise. The dance also functions as a symbolic commemoration of the destruction of the Yadav dynasty, represented through the rhythmic use of pestles.

How it is danced involves a structured progression through the village geography. The performance begins at the site of a former Shiva temple, which was converted into a church during the period of religious conversions in Goa. Dancers organize themselves into two parallel rows, stepping forward to a specific beat while carrying their pestles. A unique feature of the procession is the presence of a participant in a bear costume, whose leash is held by the lead dancer. Upon reaching the church square, the formation shifts into a circle. Here, the dancers move their pestles in and out of the ring in a coordinated motion that mimics the pounding of grain. This central ritual is followed by a symbolic act where a Devadasi girl sweeps the ground where the pounding occurred, after which the troupe visits individual houses to perform in their yards.

Music and instruments are central to the percussive nature of the dance. The primary prop, the musall or pestle, is not merely a wooden pole; it features holes drilled into its center containing metal blades or bells that produce a jingling sound with every movement. This is supported by a traditional ensemble consisting of the ghumot (an earthen pot drum), kansaalle (cymbals), and the dholke. The accompanying songs are part of a strictly oral tradition, passed down through generations without written records. These compositions are noted for their historical depth, containing praise for past dynasties and narratives of victory that require further analytical study to fully decode.

Costume and setting reflect the traditional attire of the region's Christian Kshatriya community. Performers wear a white dhoti paired with a long-sleeved shirt, over which a specialized black jacket is worn. The ensemble is completed with a turban, known as a pagdi. The lead dancer is distinguished by attire that differs from the rest of the troupe, marking his role in guiding the 'bear' and leading the procession. The setting is always outdoors, moving from the sacred space of the church to the domestic spaces of the village gaonkars, illuminated by torchbearers known as divtekars who dance alongside the main troupe.

Occasions and meaning have shifted slightly over time. While Mussoll was historically performed during the festival of Shigmo, it is now primarily presented on the second day of the Goa Carnival in February. Despite this shift in the festival calendar, the dance retains its character as a martial and commemorative rite. It serves as a living link to Chandor's identity as a former royal capital, ensuring that the names of the Kadamba and Vijayanagara rulers remain integrated into the village's annual cultural cycle through the rhythmic strike of the pestle.
card.sacred_note: While not restricted, the dance is a ritualized performance that begins at a church built on a former Shiva temple site and involves specific community roles.

sections.origins_and_history: Chandor, originally Chandrapur, was the capital of the Kadamba dynasty. The dance is linked to King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire, who reportedly performed it in 1390 after defeating a Chola ruler. It also commemorates the fall of the Yadav dynasty.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers form two rows and march to a specific beat, later forming a circle to simulate grain pounding with pestles. A lead dancer holds a leash attached to a participant in a bear costume. The routine includes a symbolic sweeping of the ground by a Devadasi girl.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided by the ghumot, kansaalle (jhanjh), and dholke. The pestles themselves are instruments, containing internal bells or blades. Songs are strictly oral and contain historical hymns.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a dhoti, long-sleeved shirt, black jacket, and a turban (pagdi). The dance occurs in front of the village church and in the yards of local houses, accompanied by torchbearers called divtekars.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a Shigmo tradition, it is now performed on the second day of the Goa Carnival. It serves as an artistic commemoration of historical victories and the Kadamba period.
sections.notable_figures: King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire is cited as a historical performer of the dance in 1390.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is specifically preserved in the village of Chandor in the Salcete region of Goa.
sections.lineage: The dance claims lineage from the Satavahana and Kadamba dynasties, with influences from the Vijayanagara Empire.
